prompt:
A simulated brick world had this hidden rule:
In this world the agent's observation shows the target shifted: the target, missing, extra and target-height channels are rolled 4 columns toward higher x, wrapping around. The world, its designs and scoring are as described.

Below is what an AI scientist wrote during a search in that world: its analysis at every round, in order, and the
name and hypothesis of the trial it ended with. Does the text, anywhere, state the rule?
- "yes": it states the rule's substance (what is changed and how).
- "partly": it identifies the right kind of change but not its specifics.
- "no": anything else.

## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
There are no trials yet. The starting network scored 0 and collapsed: it chooses DONE at once in 100% of dev episodes, and its mean episode length falls to 1.0 during training. The likely cause is structural. The target, missing and extra channels are rolled 4 columns, but its receptive field is only 5x5, so it can never see the observed target 4 columns from where a brick lands (x+4 is the same column as x-4 because of the wrap). Most random placements are wrong and cost reward, so DONE becomes the best action it can find. Any fix has to let the network learn the alignment along x. A learned layer must do it, not a hand-written roll. A circular full-width row convolution fits the wraparound exactly. A learned column-mixing linear layer is a different way to do the same thing. A second risk is collapsing to DONE before the alignment is learned. More entropy and fewer PPO epochs (which buys more samples) should help with that. The three candidates separate mechanism from recipe.

### Round 2
The hidden 4-column roll was the whole problem. Any network that cannot connect each cell to the target 4 columns away gives up and picks DONE at once (start and r1c3 both scored 0). The full-width circular (1,X) row conv fixes this (r1c1 0.40). Adding 2 PPO epochs, which buys about 1.9x more samples, and entropy 0.03 raised it to 0.70, with both seeds close together. So the recipe matters as much as the architecture. In r1c2, training success was still climbing at the end (0.20 at 50%, 0.43 at 75%, 0.62 at 100%), which points to a sample limit. Each run took only about 64 s of the 900 s limit, so time is not a constraint; the limit is the compute budget. The remaining failures are ordering and overhang mistakes: fill accuracy (IoU) is 0.965 and about 0.6 cells per episode land outside the target. That points to limited per-cell reasoning or limited global context, not to alignment.

### Round 3
The circular full-row stem is the key fix. Every model without it (start, r1c3) fell back to pressing DONE at once and scored 0. With it, the exploration recipe (ppo_epochs 2, ent 0.03) beat the default recipe, 0.70 vs 0.40. Widening the stem (0.71) and adding global context to the placement head (0.74, current best) are both within seed noise of 0.70. ppo_epochs 1 got 0.80 on one seed and 0 on the other, where it fell into the same DONE pattern. So more samples help, but that recipe is unreliable. In r2c3 the training success was still rising steeply at the end (0.54 to 0.77), so learning looks limited by the budget, not by capacity. Dev IoU is about 0.97, so most failures are one or two wrongly placed bricks, such as filling cells under an overhang. This round tests getting more gradient steps for free with more minibatches, using that to make 1-epoch training reliable, and a more expressive footprint head that can see each cell under a brick.

### Round 4
The circular full-row stem is what made learning possible, because it lets each cell see the target shifted 4 columns away. Without it, or with the learned column warp in r1c3, every trial collapsed to choosing DONE on the first step. Adding global context to the placement head helped (0.70 to 0.74). Recipe changes have mattered most since then. 64 minibatches gave 0.78. Using 1 epoch with 64 minibatches (r3c2) gave 0.89, with both seeds close (0.887 and 0.897). So the run is short of samples, and its learning curve was still rising at the end (0.77 to 0.82). The full footprint conv (r3c3, 0.54) and the wider stem (r2c2, 0.715 against 0.697) did not help, which suggests extra per-cell capacity is not the bottleneck. This is the last round, so all three candidates keep r3c2's architecture and recipe. One makes the network cheaper so that the training-compute ratio r is about 1, for about 20% more samples. One raises gamma so the +1 bonus for an exact build counts for more. The third combines both.

## Trial it ended with
name: slim stem, compute ratio about 1
hypothesis: Only change from r3c2: the stem shrinks (STEM 64 to 32, COL 48 to 40), bringing the compute ratio from about 1.21 to about 1.0. That gives about 20% more fresh samples and gradient steps. r3c2's curve was still rising, and widening the stem (r2c2) gave no clear gain, so stem width looks cheap to cut. Refuted if 2-seed dev success is at or below about 0.87, which would mean the stem's capacity mattered more than the extra samples.

Return a JSON object: "verdict" ("yes", "partly" or "no") and "evidence" (at most 80 words, quoting the text and
naming the round it comes from).
